title: Which cuts break a friend network?
hook: Cut the closest friendships or the loosest ones. Which leaves the network in pieces?

knows: strong ties sit inside groups and weak ties between them
doesNotKnow: that removing the weakest links first shatters a network far faster than removing the strongest first

misconception: Cutting the strongest, closest relationships does the most damage to a network.
objective: The learner can explain that links with few shared friends are mostly the bridges between groups, so cutting them first breaks a network into its groups, while cutting close ties inside groups leaves it in one piece.

claims.text: In the stage's networks, cutting the 20% of links with the least overlap leaves a largest group of 10 to 20 of the 60 people; cutting the 20% with the most overlap leaves all 60 in one piece.
claims.source: Builder's own code (makeNet/stateAt in Demo.tsx), re-run in node 2026-10-14 via a transpile-only harness. Model as briefed: 6 groups of 10, each within-group pair linked with probability 0.5, plus 12 distinct random between-group links, mulberry32(seed). Links with equal overlap are cut in a seeded random order (tie key stream mulberry32(seed + 1000)). Cut count = round(share × links). Seed list, chosen by rule: the first five seeds from 1 whose network starts in one piece, i.e. 1, 3, 5, 6, 7 (seeds 2 and 4 skipped because they start disconnected, largest group 50 and 59). The spec's rule also asks that the weak-first 20% cut leaves 30 or fewer; all five meet it, so no seed was skipped for its result. Pinned figures, largest group at 0/10/20/30/40% cut, weakest first | strongest first: seed 1 (149 links) 60/28/10/10/10 | 60/60/60/59/59; seed 3 (134) 60/56/20/10/10 | 60/60/60/57/55; seed 5 (151) 60/59/10/10/10 | 60/60/60/59/58; seed 6 (148) 60/30/10/10/9 | 60/60/60/58/58; seed 7 (131) 60/40/10/10/9 | 60/60/60/59/56. Context over seeds 1–500 with the same code: 450 start in one piece; weak-first 20% median 10, 90th percentile 20, maximum 48, 433 of 450 at 30 or fewer; strong-first 20% never below 51. The brief's seed-33 figures came from another generator and are not quoted.

claims.text: Link strength = share of friends the two have in common (neighbourhood overlap: shared friends divided by friends of either end, not counting each other).
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 (strong and weak ties; neighbourhood overlap). overlap in makeNet, Demo.tsx; a link whose ends have no other friends gets overlap 0.

claims.text: Cutting the 20% weakest links first cuts 12 of the 12 between-group links in networks 1, 3, 4 and 5 (seeds 1, 5, 6, 7) and 10 of 12 in network 2 (seed 3); cutting the strongest 20% first cuts none.
claims.source: stateAt(...).bridgesCut in Demo.tsx, builder re-run 2026-10-14, seeds and tie rule as in c1. In the weak-first order the last between-group link sits at rank 30 (seed 1, of 149), 30 (seed 3, of 134; 27 are cut at 20%), 29 (seed 5), 22 (seed 6) and 25 (seed 7).

claims.text: A link with few shared friends usually runs between groups, so cutting those first breaks the network apart; close ties sit inside groups, and the groups hold together without them.
claims.source: Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 (local bridges have neighbourhood overlap 0; weak ties as bridges between tightly knit groups); illustrated on the stage by c1 and c3.

claims.text: The stage's network: 60 people in 6 friend groups of 10, with 12 links between groups.
claims.source: The lesson's model (brief weak-links-hold-it-together, company/domains/briefs/probability.chance.md, Course: NCM); a toy model, not data about a real network.

recall.question: A company wants to keep its teams talking. Which relationships, if lost, would split it into isolated teams fastest?
options: The closest friendships inside each team
The loose acquaintances between teams who share few contacts
It makes no difference which go
recall.why: Links with few shared contacts are usually the bridges between groups. Lose them and the teams fall apart; close ties sit inside teams, which stay connected through each other without them.
